name: GNU Bash
summary: A POSIX-oriented command shell whose reader/parser produces command structures for execution, with pipelines, job control, shell variables, functions, and builtins sharing shell process state.

features.name: Reader, parser, and executor pipeline
features.description: Bash's fixed source implements a reader loop that reads commands, uses a generated parser to build command structures, and dispatches them through execute_command_internal. The Bash Reference Manual describes shell operation as reading, parsing, expanding, and executing commands.
benefits: Separates syntax recognition from execution and expansion
Supports interactive and non-interactive input through a common shell loop
costs: Shell grammar, expansion rules, and execution contexts are tightly coupled
Recursive evaluation paths such as command substitution increase control-flow complexity

features.name: Pipeline and job-control process model
features.description: The source builds process pipelines, assigns process groups when job control is enabled, tracks jobs, and waits for or reports their state. The Bash manual documents pipelines, asynchronous commands, and job-control behavior.
benefits: Composes commands through Unix pipes and asynchronous process groups
Tracks process completion and foreground/background status at the shell boundary
costs: Signals, terminal ownership, and wait status are platform-sensitive
Pipeline failures and asynchronous completion require shared job bookkeeping

features.name: Shell variable, function, and builtin state
features.description: Bash stores scalar, indexed-array, and associative-array variables in shell contexts, exports selected state, and executes builtins and functions within the shell process. The manual documents shell parameters, arrays, functions, and builtin commands.
benefits: Builtins and functions can mutate shell state without an external process boundary
Structured variables and dynamic scopes support reusable scripts
costs: State visibility and context restoration vary across subshell and function boundaries
A large builtin and compatibility surface constrains language evolution

mathematical_views.question: How does input become parsed command structure, expanded words, execution effects, and an exit status?
assumptions: Input passes through reading, parsing, expansion, and execution stages
Execution may recurse for substitutions, functions, and sourced files
The view abstracts generated parser implementation details and OS scheduling

mathematical_views.question: How do shell contexts, builtins, functions, process groups, pipes, and jobs connect?
assumptions: Shell variables and process groups are distinct resource classes
Edges represent data flow, state mutation, fork/exec, or wait relationships
The graph does not imply that all pipeline stages share shell variable state

benefits: One shell loop supports scripts and interactive commands
costs: Expansion and recursive evaluation increase semantic coupling

benefits: Unix process composition and foreground control
costs: Signals, terminal state, and waits complicate portability

benefits: Scripts can mutate shell state directly
costs: Scope and compatibility rules make state behavior subtle
